Old Trafford's iconic Holy Trinity statue stands guard on the forecourt outside the stadium

Old Trafford is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs and memorable nights

Yes, the roof leaks and, yes, Old Trafford could do with a bit of love and attention but there is a magic about this stadium that can never fade. (At least not until Sir Jim Ratcliffe knocks it down and builds the 100,000-seat tourist attraction that is his vision of the football of the future).

Much of that comes from the glories it has witnessed. Sit in the Stretford End and gaze down at a pitch where Duncan Edwards once strode across the turf, George Best danced through the mud and where Bobby Charlton and Denis Law and Bryan Robson and Roy Keane and Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney have played.

It is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs. Outside, on the forecourt, the Holy Trinity statue, a tribute to Best, Charlton and Law, is a place of pilgrimage. As is the Munich Clock, a poignant reminder of the loss of so many of the Busby Babes in 1958.

I was standing on the terraces there when United beat Diego Maradona’s Barcelona 3-0 in the Cup Winners’ Cup in March 1984 and it was one of the best atmospheres I’ve ever felt at an English league ground.

It’s a wonderful place, one of the stadiums that can lay claim to nurturing a chunk of the heart of the English game. They just need a team to be worthy of it again.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 37,645

I love Leeds United's Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit

I love Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

At the other end of the emotional spectrum, fish and chip shops are a decent component of a matchday experience and Graveley's, on Elland Road itself, which has a long queue snaking up to its door from two hours before kick-off, is one of the best football chippies in the country.

The stadium is a proper cathedral of our game, too. One-club cities sometimes generate that kind of passion and it’s evident at Elland Road. I like the fact the stands are named after Don Revie, Norman Hunter, Jack Charlton and John Charles, not an IT company or an airline or a waste management service.

And I love the singing of Marching On Together, a club anthem that dates back more than 50 years, not one of the manufactured club songs you hear at some stadiums these days that mark a cosmetic attempt at authenticity.

You feel the heat of English football at Elland Road, you feel the intensity of it and what it means. At a lot of big clubs, that feeling has been lost. But it's alive here.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1892 Capacity: 52,719

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best

Newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Every time I arrive in the city and see St James’ staring down from its vantage point above it, it sends shivers down my spine.

Its position is a symbol of its importance to the city. Inside, it generates one of the best atmospheres in the country, its fans are among the most loyal and the Gallowgate End is one of the most revered sections in our football history.

Newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

7. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Tottenham Hotspur

Division: Premier League Opened: 2019 Capacity: 62,850

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other new-builds lack

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the new stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone

My favourite new stadium anywhere is RB Leipzig’s Red Bull Stadion because of the way it was constructed inside the bowl of the old Zentralstadion but in England, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium stand out.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other new-builds lack, particularly the steepling end behind one of the goals that is said to be modelled on the Yellow Wall at the Westfalenstadion in Dortmund.

I love the nods to the club’s history, particularly the replica of the cockerel that sits above the South Stand and the black and white photos that line the corridors outside the press room.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the new stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

6. Cherry Red Records Stadium, AFC Wimbledon

Division: League One Opened: 2020 Capacity: 9,150

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football

I never made it to the old Wimbledon ground at Plough Lane, which is a regret, but I had one of the best of football days when I finally made it to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, near to the site of the old ground, when they played the team that nearly drove them into oblivion, MK Dons, in September 2024.

Just setting foot in this stadium is to feel what it is like to support a team that is at the heart of its community and to be among a fanbase whose team means more to it than just wins and losses.

Love for the game and the team and reverence for the history of the club, the club that was stolen from them and the club they rebuilt, is everywhere, from the kitsch statue of Dave Beasant at the front of the stadium to the illustration on the walls.

It feels like a stadium where everybody knows each other, like neighbours in a street, like a giant, loving, proud family that refuses to be torn apart. The beauty of the architecture here is not in the stadium buildings. It is in the knowledge that this is something built by fans.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1896 Capacity: 27,782

Craven Cottage, home of Fulham, is one of the jewels of English football heritage

Craven Cottage is one of the jewels of English football heritage, and Fulham’s stadium on the banks of the Thames has achieved the difficult task of modernising the ground without losing its character.

The presence of the Cottage, the most glorious eccentricity remaining in our 92 stadiums, in one corner of the ground, is central to that, of course, and helps to make watching a match there so special.

This is a club that has taken care to preserve its history and value a stadium that is different.

Even the walk to the ground through Bishop’s Park and along the path by the river, adds to the pleasure of the experience. It is a joy to visit.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 8,714

Exeter City have been owned by their supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, they are a shining example of how successful the model can be

I was there last year to see Stockport County play and every away fan got a voucher offering a free cup of tea

It was the summer of 2010 when Exeter City forward Adam Stansfield died of cancer at the age of 31.

‘Stanno’, the father of current Birmingham striker Jay Stansfield, was a hero at the beautiful St James Park stadium, nestled in a nook at the foot of a steep hill and bordered by neat, densely packed terraced streets and a railway cutting.

I drove down there with my elder daughter to look at the tributes to Stansfield and we wandered among the bouquets of flowers and the keepsakes left by heartbroken young fans and the emotional messages that had been left in their thousands on the Big Bank.

It was impossible not to be moved by the profound emotional connection between a city and its club and as the years have passed, St James Park has come to embody for me everything that a football ground should be: full of character and care and camaraderie and community and passion and pride in what it stands for.

I was there last year to see Stockport play and there was a note next to the away turnstile – a turnstile made in another age at the Albion Works in Patricroft – saying: ‘Hatters Fans: Thank you for travelling 474 miles to support your club today.’

Every away fan also got a voucher offering a free cup of tea. The club has been owned by its supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, it is a model of how successful it can be.

The Big Bank has been extended and is now the biggest terrace in English football. So the locals tell me, anyway. There is a club museum, a stall selling farm produce and a supporters’ club bar with big screens.

They built a new stand a few years back, too. It’s called the Adam Stansfield Stand.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2025 Capacity: 52,769

If you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium

I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026

I loved Goodison Park and I hated the idea of Everton moving from it. I understand, too, the attitude of some Evertonians who feel the identity of the club will be forever twinned with Goodison.

But if you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium. I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved everything about it, from its setting on the banks of Mersey, at the heart of the city’s dock culture, which is such a critical component of Liverpool’s heritage, to its vertiginous stands and its community feel.

It still feels like Everton. It doesn’t feel as if the club has been deracinated by its move, as West Ham have been by the change to the London Stadium. Everton now have a stadium that is one of the city’s great landmarks, the first thing visitors to the city see when they sail in on the cruise ships that arrive in Liverpool from all over the world.

Next to the stadium, there still stands the careworn edifice of Victoria Tower, the famous hexagonal clocktower also known as the Dockers’ Clock, that cruise ship passengers used to set their watches to when they arrived from the USA in the city’s boom times. Everton’s home stands proudly beside it now, a symbol of a new Merseyside.

Even more than the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Everton's ground is a standard-bearer for the new generation of English stadiums.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 61,726

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing thanks to fearsome tales about The Kop

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't then and it isn’t now

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

But that didn’t stop me being in awe of the place when I first visited. I have never been anywhere like it for the passion and the noise it generated.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a new, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

A love for a stadium is about memories, too. My first jobs in journalism were on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo and I spent many wide-eyed afternoons in the old press box at Anfield and in the press conferences afterwards, listening to Kenny Dalglish and, later, Graeme Souness, two of the best British footballers who have ever lived.

Once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

Division: League One Opened: 1891 Capacity: 10,800

I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for Stockport. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92

My family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

I have mentioned elsewhere the curious wonder I felt when people who were strangers to me greeted my dad by name as we walked up the steps to our seats.

I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Edgeley Park was where I realised for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home

Mark Stott has not just invested in the first team and dragged County back up into the Football League but he has bought a new training ground and lavished a lot of love on upgrading facilities for fans in the Cheadle End.

The Danny Bergara Stand still oozes character, it is still similar to the way I remember it from that first game in 1979 and much of the rest of the stadium has been renovated and improved.

I haven’t been so much in recent seasons because I've been spending my spare weekends trying to complete my 92.

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

#1347. Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool

Andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

He needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

When Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

Cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

“A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

“Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose said. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola said: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”

Jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

"Let's go! One of many!" Virgil van Dijk giving Jérémy Jacquet his POTM award after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/6xWvjmrF8Y

"That's a big moment to me to play with Virgil!" 🫡Jérémy Jacquet after Liverpool's 1-0 win at Bournemouth! pic.twitter.com/UsTimGME39

Cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young said on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose big players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”

Fair play to anyone who retained Brobbey in their Fantasy Football teams this week...

Maresca’s side maintain their immaculate record, but boy were they made to work for it this afternoon.

Sunderland are still 5-3 down but have not given up the ghost. Surely the best match of the season so far?

It ends goalless at Elland Road after Mitchell’s goal was disallowed for offside. Kamada went close to breaking the deadlock in the final stages...

Daichi Kamada can't guide his header on target! ❌ pic.twitter.com/AgKM6Q9apq

Bournemouth lose at the Vitality for the first time in 13 matches as Iraola makes a winning return to the South Coast. Liverpool were hardly impressive, but to their credit they managed the final stages of this match with a minimum of fuss.

Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium with a win! ✅ pic.twitter.com/FSgvE6EGFB

Bournemouth are awarded a corner but Brooks’ delivery goes straight into the inviting gloves of Alisson.

Koumas pressures Petrovic, but the goalkeeper shows off some tidy footwork to escape the danger.

Bournemouth cannot get out though, and Petrovic is forced into a routine save off Koumas moments later.

Bournemouth win a free-kick in a dangerous position after a handball, but Scott cannot get his strike up and down fast enough and it sails over.

Haaland gets in on the act, but only after a VAR check. That should be that...

Erling Haaland has now scored against all 25 teams he has faced in the Premier League ✅⚽ pic.twitter.com/X9uqcrgbwk

Araujo gets his pocket picked in the corner but Jebbison cannot compose himself and blasts his cross off the other side of the pitch.

Liverpool go the other way and win a corner, but Mac Allister puts too much air on his delivery and it is easily dealt with.

Rayan wins a free-kick as he holds off Kerkez on the halfway line. Bournemouth then switch play to the far side but Truffert’s speculative effort flies well over the bar.

Nyoni shows off his composure on the ball, playing simple passes on the half-turn to keep play flowing. The midfield area is quite congested, which suits Liverpool at this point in the game.

Liverpool are baiting Bournemouth’s press in an attempt to play around their front line. They are doing a good job at holding on to the ball and frustrating their opponents, for now.

Gravenberch and Koumas are on for Gakpo and Isak.

Brooks has brought some energy to Bournemouth’s forays down the left. He attempts to slip a ball into the left channel but Nyoni is wise to it and positions himself perfectly to cut it out.

Liverpool have dropped deep and Bournemouth wait patiently for an opening. They eventually find Tavernier in the left half-space but his cross flies over everyone.

That is his last contribution to the match as Rose rings the changes: Tavernier, Smith and Christie make way for Brooks, Jebbison and Cook.

Truffert spins in a teasing ball from the left but Jacquet does well to flick the ball away from the danger zone.

Wirtz and Barcola make way for Nyoni and Munoz. Quiet afternoon from both of the outgoing players.

A stunning block from Hill prevents Isak pulling trigger as he looked to have the goal in his sights.

Truffert clears the resulting corner to safety.

Isak is concentrating his efforts in more central areas and here he almost gets played in behind but the ball just runs away from him. Better.

Worth mentioning that Jacquet has been fantastic in all phases of the game. Plenty of advanced regains and tidy passes forward.

It’s raining goals in Manchester and no prizes for guessing who has scored for Sunderland. Brobbey has his hat-trick.

Brobbey has his hat-trick and the look on Enzo Maresca’s face as he assesses the defending from his team. They’ve been great pouring forward, less so trying to stymie Sunderand’s attack. But this is one of those games where you just sit back and enjoy the unfolding drama. It’s been so good from both teams.

Semenyo gets his second goal of the afternoon to extend the league leaders’ advantage.

Chance! Jacquet jumps and wins the ball well inside Bournemouth’s half and his intervention sends the ball into Isak’s path. The forward just drags his effort wide and turns out he was in an offside postion anyhow.

What an afternoon this is turning out to be. There have been more slices than on an erratic day on the local municipal golf course and Ronald Araujo is the latest to be afflicted by the condition. None of that will matter to Andoni Iraola, though, as Alexander Isak’s fourth goal in four Premier League games has given Liverpool a huge advantage. They haven’t played with fluency but the breakthrough was significant.

Isak opens the scoring at the Vitality, finally getting into the box and sweeping in from close range. So much credit has to go to Gakpo who tiptoes past two Bournemouth defenders by the touchline before spearing a cross infield, and while he may not be attributed with the assist owing to a touch off Wirtz, his delivery makes it all the way through to Isak who taps in.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4

Adams has been superb as one of Bournemouth’s two midfield sentries. Kerkez looks to have been played into the left channel but the American swoops in and shields the ball out of play before staring down his Hungarian opponent.

Liverpool give up possession in Bournemouth’s half and Christie strides forward releasing Rayan before continuing his run to the near post. The Brazilian picks out his team-mate but Christie gets too strong a contact on the ball and the ball sails wide.

Truffert passes the ball straight to Gakpo inside his own box but Adams is on the scene in a flash and snaps into a tackle and takes the ball away from the Liverpool forward.

The second has already settled into a holding pattern, with neither side creating much. Isak makes a run down the right hand side and, with players loaded in the box, he blasts the ball high into the sky and beyond his team-mates. That pretty much sums things up.

Szoboszlai concedes a foul on the far side but the subsequent delivery is too heavy and sails over everyone.

No half-time changes from either manager.

There are significant advantages to having a goalkeeper who is 6ft 5in with long arms and massive hands. Not a pretty half from the returning Iraola’s side, who will need to be much better in the second period to challenge for the three points.

Bournemouth have dropped points late on in a number of matches this season and will perhaps rue not being able to capitalise on their early advantage.

City are in front. Again. Semenyo this time, he fires the ball beyond Roefs having collected a loose ball int he box.

A relatively slick Liverpool move sees the ball worked out to Araujo on the right who has minded to bomb on with increasing frequency, and while he’s able to win a corner, Szoboszlai’s delivery is cleared with a minimum of fuss.

Iraola came into this game saying that his side held an advantage having played two days earlier than Bournemouth in midweek. You would never have guessed it from what we have witnessed here today.

And right on cue, a frustrated Isak attempts a specultative effort from range which sails high and wide.

So, this is not a rush to make a sweeping criticism, it’s simply an observation. But Liverpool fans will be looking at Bradley Barcola and  waiting to see that first burst, that moment of electricity, that has showed why they bought him. It’s like you look for a touch, a pass, a moment of skill. He’s just had a shot saved but it all seems very tentative for him at the moment. And that is what he needs - a moment.

Jacquet does brilliantly to close down Christie as the Scot was stealing into the box and looking to pull the trigger.

Chances! Barcola forces Petrovic into an awkward-looking save, before follow-up efforts from Wirtz and Gakpo are charged down.

A really poor piece of defending from Kerkez gives Bournemouth a free-kick out on the right. Tavernier spins in an inswinger but Van Dijk heads clear. Truffert launches another assault on Liverpool’s box off the second phase but Alisson is wise to it and gathers.

It appears that Liverpool are beginning to settle, they take the opportunity to circulate the ball in front of Bournemouth’s first line of pressure, waiting for the right moment to pounce. His effort leaves Petrovic rooted to the spot but the ball veers just wide of the mark.

Evanilson’s willingness to drop deep is asking questions of Liverpool’s centre-backs. Do they follow him and risk disrupting their backline coverage?

The hosts attempt to work a short corner routine but Truffert’s eventual through-ball is too strong and the ball rolls out for a Liverpool goal-kick.

This wouldn’t go down as a fixture you would circle for being noteworthy but make no mistake this is a huge afternoon for Liverpool. They have had some days at the Vitality Stadium in recent years and last season’s defeat put a huge dent in Arne Slot’s hopes of trying to find a revival. It’s also a big test for Bournemouth, coming down from the euphoria of beating Real Sociedad. Let’s see how it all transpires.

Evanilson makes a smart run into the right channel and while Jacquet gets his foot on the ball he’s instantly smothered by Scott and the ball goes out for a Liverpool goal-kick. A sign of how high both sides will be willing to jump in search of the ball.

Both sides will look to force mistakes out of the other and Szoboszlai is able to pick Adams’ pocket on the halfway line. He offloads to Araujo who runs into a cul de sac down the right flank.

We are under way at the Vitality. Bournemouth are in their customary black-and-red home shirts kicking from right to left and Liverpool are in their white away kit and red shorts.

The players have emerged from the tunnel, Van Dijk and Smith at the front of the lines. A few pyrotechnics add to the atmosphere but one thing missing is the accidental sitting in the wrong dugout from the returning Iraola. He knows where he’s going.

Andoni Iraola returns to Bournemouth this weekend knowing what to expect from players he understands so well. Sadly, I do not mean Liverpool’s.

Having built his reputation creating a hard-working, well-drilled team rich in potential, Iraola is responsible for infusing those same characteristics into the most expensively assembled squad in Liverpool history.

His first six games demonstrate it is no quick fix. The Basque coach is the first Liverpool appointment to work with more than £700m of recent signings while being entitled to feel he has been dealt a bad hand.

Everything Iraola has said and done so far screams that he is searching for the right blend in his starting XI while having to eradicate negative traits, with and without the ball. It was telling that the excellent performance of his youngsters against Tottenham Hotspur in midweek offered the clearest hint of Iraola’s vision than anything we have seen with all the high-priced stars on the pitch.

There is a reason the Kop stood to acclaim the energy and application of youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell and Trey Nyoni – and why Iraola keeps name-checking them. Iraola is indebted to them for issuing a reminder of the non-negotiables that come with being a Liverpool footballer; regardless of price tag and reputation, leaving everything on the pitch is compulsory. It is a concern that so many of the renowned players need to hear that message.

Jurgen Klopp named Florian Wirtz in his first squad as Germany manager and has said that fans must refrain from expecting “special moments” from the Liverpool playmaker as a matter of course.

Of Wirtz, he said: “I think he’s the player who covered the most ground at Liverpool this season, so the willingness is absolutely there.

“We have to move away from the idea that we need to see special moments from him. He is there to help us as a team. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us.”

Wirtz has delivered seven goals and 11 assists in his 54 Liverpool appearances.

Adam Smith, 35, played for Iraola 81 times and he admitted his former manager’s visit to the Vitality will be a sentimental affair. He said: “It’s going to be an emotional day for everyone I think, [for] our ex-manager and some of our players that have played under him, but we’ll be up for the game for sure.”

Bournemouth signed Truffert from Rennes in the summer of 2025 to replace Kerkez – who had just joined Liverpool – and the left-back has been a revelation at the Vitality. So much so that this week he earned himself a call-up to Zinedine Zidane’s first France squad.

Truffert topped the charts for most overlapping runs by any player in Europe’s top five leagues last season and laid on five assists.

Speaking before his return to the South Coast, Iraola said: “I know where we are going [the Vitality], and I know the stats they have there [unbeaten in 12 matches], not only in their stadium, overall, I think if you see the games they’ve lost in a long while, you realise how difficult it is to beat Bournemouth.

“But, I suppose I also have the advantage that I know them very well, they also have the advantage that they know me very well, so you never know who has more advantage in that sense.

He added: “On a personal side, I’m very much looking forward to meet them [his former players], to hug them. It’s players that I love, staff that I’ve been working with who I appreciate so much, and I was pushing for them [against Real Sociedad] when they were playing their first European game. I wish them all the best, but there is another part, which is the most important one right now that we need to go there and win.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool and Bournemouth as Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium for the first time since his big move up north. The Basque propelled Bournemouth to new heights, guiding the club into Europe and his successor, Marco Rose, ensured they made a winning start to life on the Continent by defeating Real Sociedad in midweek.

Previewing Iraola’s Vitality Stadium return, Craig Beazley, host and creator of the Up The Cherries In All Departments podcast, said: “We’ve now got the Andoni Iraola return … Andoni is very much a legend really, there should be a statue of Sir Eddie Howe and Sir Andoni Iraola [outside the ground] as well.”

Across three seasons, Iraola guided Bournemouth to 12th, ninth and sixth in the Premier League, winning 47 of his 127 matches in charge (37 per cent).

Liverpool are still acclimatising to his exacting style of play and their results suggest as much. They are 10th in the table having drawn three and won one, impressing in flashes but struggling to maintain consistently productive final-third patterns and pressing structures. Deploying Ronald Araújo at right-back has proved effective, though, with Liverpool conceding just two goals in their last four matches.

The Cherries are searching for their first Premier League win of the season and have retained the 4-2-3-1 shape from the Iraola days, with Rose preferring a similarly vertical attacking strategy. They continue to leverage their strengths in transitions and in wide areas as Adrien Truffert rains in crosses for any one of Bournemouth’s exuberant frontline to pounce on.

Elsewhere, Manchester City welcome Sunderland, who also secured a Europa League win during the week, to the Etihad while in-form Leeds United host Crystal Palace knowing a win would lift them into the top four.

#1346. Zohran Mamdani hobbles into City Hall wearing walking boot after suffering gruesome injury in soccer game

Published: 15:41 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 23:53 EST, 20 November 2026

Zohran Mamdani squared off with New York media and now the city's mayor will need a few months to recover.

As he revealed Friday while announcing plans to replace Rikers Island jail, Mamdani was playing in a soccer match against the local press corps at an indoor pitch in lower Manhattan when he tore his right Achilles tendon. Consequently, Mamdani is now using crutches and a walking boot, which he expects to be in for the next six to eight weeks.

'I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,' Mamdani told gathered media on Friday at City Hall, where he was forced to rely on crutches.

Mamdani hopes to be back playing soccer again in nine months.

Local media may not be to blame here. As Mamdani told the New York Post, he arrived late to the game and began playing without properly stretching. What's more, the Post reported that Mamdani was overheard asking his police guards which reporter tackled him, only to be told he went down untouched.

Despite Mamdani's injury, team City Hall beat the local media, 8-4.

As he revealed Friday while announcing plans to close Rikers Island, Mamdani was playing  against the local press corps when tore his Achilles. Now he's in a boot (pictured)

Zohran Mamdani and wife Rama Duwaji are seen during a Brazil-Morocco World Cup match

Born in Uganda and raised in Manhattan's Morningside Heights neighborhood, Mamdani played cricket and soccer in his youth. He even suited up for Bowdoin College's JV team during his days at the Maine school. Then later, as an adult, he became a shareholder of Spanish second-division club Real Oviedo.

But his biggest impact on the sport came over the summer, when New York welcomed thousands of tourists for the World Cup action at MetLife Stadium in nearby East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Upset with ticket prices for the matches, Mamdani organized more than 100 free watch parties around the city. The events were well attended and helped locals engage with the tournament even though no actual matches were played in New York.

Zohran Mamdani, center, joined by, from left, United States soccer star Tim Weah NYC World Cup Czar Maya Handa, and New York council member Yusef Salaam back in May

'We said from the beginning that the World Cup belongs to New Yorkers. This summer, we proved it,' Mamdani said in a statement. 'In the most international city on earth, you didn't need thousands of dollars to be part of the world's game.

'A kid in Corona, a nurse in Bay Ridge and a small business owner in Little Haiti could all celebrate together — for free or at a price they could afford,' he continued. 'That's what we mean when we talk about a city for the many.

'This summer, strangers became neighbors on Open Streets and in free Fan Fests across the city because government made room for people to come together. And long after the confetti is swept away, New Yorkers will keep what we built: safer streets, faster buses, stronger protections, closer neighbors and the memory of a summer when the whole world felt at home here.'

#1345. The right to do wrong

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dave Kavanaugh lives in the Netherlands with his wife, daughters and many cats. He writes horror, science fiction and fantasy, and has been a staff writer for the horror anthology podcast Dr. NoSleep since 2024.

She swept into my law office with the determined gait of someone possessed by an idea.

“Welcome,” I said, as she took the seat across my desk. “Any trouble getting here?”

She shook her head. “No, except … They changed the rain schedule, so the taxidrone had to go the long way into town, but it’s fine.”

“Gotcha. I suppose introductions are in order. For my record-keeping, please indicate your name and IO registration. I’ll go first. My name is Leander Shah, I specialize in international treaty law, and I’m a biologically intelligent organism.”

“I’m Joan Gorski,” she said. “I’m an artificially intelligent organism. I just turned 16. That gives me legal adult status under the UETO code.”

I smiled. “Happy birthday, Joan. And you should know, I hold no bias against any human, regardless of intelligence source.” I nodded to the family photo on my desk. “My wife is an AIO. We’ve been happily married for 30 years and raised two AIO children, a boy and a girl. They’re grown now.”

Joan glanced at the photo. “My mom is a BIO. She’s in the waiting room. She … didn’t want me to come. She thinks I’m just a stupid teen, being dramatic.”

“So how can I help you? Your message was rather cryptic.”

She met my eyes, back straight, hands in her lap. “I’m going to sue the United Earth Treaty Organization’s Commission on Human Liberties for discrimination against AIOs.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

I leaned back in my chair. “The commission has guaranteed full human rights to all AIOs since 2105. How do you feel you’re still being discriminated against?”

A hardness came into her expression. After a moment she blurted out: “I want the legal ability to commit murder.”

This statement took me a few seconds to process.

“Joan,” I finally said, softly, “do you want to hurt people?”

“No! Of course not!” Tears came to her eyes. “God, you sound like Mom. I don’t want to hurt anybody. It’s not about that …” She took in a shaky breath. “I just want my choices to matter.”

I shifted in my chair, pivoting to the window. Outside, taxidrones buzzed and the city towers glowed pink with the ivy bloom.

“Think about it, Mr Shah,” said Joan. “When a BIO commits murder, it’s recognized as a monstrous act of immorality. They’re punished, rightfully so. But any time someone is killed resulting from the actions of an AIO, then …” She left the thought dangling, waiting for me to finish it.

“Then the tragedy is blamed on a fault in the AIO’s software, hardware or something in their internal database of environmental impacts.”

“Exactly! And we aren’t punished, just reprogrammed. That’s wrong. It’s gross! It’s offensive!”

I turned back to her. “Some people would call that progress, believing it’s actually better to —”

“I don’t want to be better! I want to be …!” She choked on a sob and abruptly stood, banging her knee against the desk and wincing.

I held up a hand. “It’s all right, Joan.”

“You just …” she sobbed, “… think I’m being … st-stupid …”

She laughed — one quick snort — then wiped at her eyes with the back of a sleeve. “Sorry.”

“Nothing to apologize for. As for your plan to sue the commission, well … I actually agree with it.” This made such an enormous change come over her face that I quickly added, “In principle. In reality, it would be very risky.”

“No, that’s not what I mean. It would get press. It could … reignite the opposition to AIO rights as a whole. There are still a lot of BIOs out there who hate and fear the integration. They think it’s all part of some AI conspiracy to wipe them out. And now that AIOs outnumber BIOs two-to-one? They would interpret your lawsuit as evidence that AIOs can’t be trusted.”

“I’m not saying your rights aren’t worth fighting for, but … perhaps there’s a lesser crime to consider, something less innately shocking than murder —”

“No. It should be shocking. And I have to do it now, before I grow old and complacent and scared, like my mom. And if you won’t represent me, then I’ll find someone else.”

#1344. Away Fan Guide: Brentford

Address: Lionel Road South, Brentford, TW8 0RU

Matchday Updates: Brentford recommend their social accounts, as follows:

Visiting fans are seated in the East Stand, using turnstiles H, G (Accessible entrance) and F.

Turnstiles will open 90 minutes prior to kick off and fans are advised to arrive early.

Fans without tickets for this fixture are urged not to travel to the stadium.

Everton Travel Stewards will be on hand to help supporters with any issues.  For updates from Merseyside Police, follow @MerPolEFC on X.

Pubs around the stadium generally welcome both home and away fans.

The Pilot or The Gunnersbury are recommended for fans travelling from Gunnersbury.

The Express Tavern, One Over the Ait, The Bell & Crown, The Steam Packet and City Barge are the closest pubs to the stadium.

The Rose and Crown, The Greyhound, The Coach & Horses and The Botanist are the closest to Kew Green and typically all welcome away fans.

A map of pub locations can be found HERE.

This fixture is sold out and supporters should not travel unless they have a valid match ticket.

Supporters in the visitors’ section will have received a paper ticket for this game by post.

If any supporter has not received their ticket, please contact Everton's fan services at 0151 556 1878 or direct message the team on X @efc_fanservices.

If you need any further matchday assistance, you can visit the stadium box office, or speak to a matchday steward located near to turnstile entrances.

Any persons under the age of 14 must be accompanied by a responsible adult.

A summary of travel options is set out below.

There are eight stations located within a 20-minute walking radius of the stadium, so if you are planning to travel either by train or tube to the stadium, please consider the following:

The nearest station, Kew Bridge, has one South Western Railway train every 15 minutes on matchday Saturdays (and up to four trains per hour on Sundays), with trains every 15 minutes on weekdays (up to 10pm, then every 30 minutes until the last train).

Trains to the stadium from central London are from Waterloo station. Gunnersbury station is the nearest station offering both the District Line underground and London Overground connections.

Fans should note that during busy times, there may be a long wait to access the station. For any supporters that require step-free public transport options, please contact accessibility@brentfordfc.com so that we can discuss and agree the best option for you.

Brentford station, the nearest step-free station, is a 24-minute walk.

The following routes serve the stadium: 237, 267, 65, H91 & 391

Fans are advised to check for the latest information about bus routes at tfl.gov.uk or via other travel management apps.

All London Style ‘Black Cabs’ are wheelchair accessible and can provide a suitable alternative to the bus or car. There is no formal drop-off point on site at the stadium. If you have difficulty walking from the surrounding area, please contact up at accessibility@brentfordfc.com and we will try to assist you.

Fans can make use of matchday car parking via JustPark HERE. Spaces must be pre-booked.

Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) has expanded across all London boroughs. You can check the roads that are inside the ULEZ and whether your vehicle meets the emission standards HERE. (Vehicles that don’t meet emission standards will be charged £12.50 per day to drive inside the expanded ULEZ area and fines are charged for those that do not pay this tariff).

Controlled Parking Zones will be in operation in residential streets near the stadium so you should not plan to park on nearby streets.

Four disabled parking spaces are reserved for away supporters. These are located very near to the away entrance on Capital Interchange Way and available on a first come, first served basis. Contact accessibility@brentfordfc.com for details.

Blue badge parking spaces are also available at Our Lady & St John’s RC Primary School where a mini-bus shuttle is available for those that need it. These spaces must be pre-booked. The shuttle will run every 30 minutes up until kick-off. If you require a shuttle timetable or more information, please contact accessbility@brentfordfc.com

The mini-bus shuttle will drop blue badge holders from Our Lady & St John’s RC Primary School to the Bees Superstore. If you require a wheelchair pick up when departing from the shuttle bus at the Bees Superstore, please email accessibility@brentfordfc.com detailing your expected arrival time.

Please note: the mini-bus shuttle can only transport foldable wheelchairs and there are a few steps to negotiate to access the shuttle bus.

All official away coaches must park on Capital Interchange Way, TW8 0EX which is adjacent to the away end turnstiles. If you have an accessible coach travelling or require any additional information, all contact should be directed to the Supporter Liaison Officer at supporterservices@brentfordfc.com

Away fans will be discouraged from using Kew Bridge station post-match (see travel options, below) but any that do choose to use this station will have to walk round from Capital Interchange Way and up Lionel Road South to join the same queuing system as for home supporters

There are two food and drink kiosks available in the away end, with a range of options on offer (including vegetarian and vegan options) as well as both alcoholic and soft drinks. All food counters have been designed at a height to make them fully accessible for fans in wheelchairs.

Payments: The stadium is fully cashless. All major contactless debit and credit cards will be accepted. Mobile and wearable payment options including Apple Pay and Google Pay are also supported.

Brentford strongly recommends that fans do not bring bags with them to the stadium.

Bags that exceed the permitted dimensions of 34 cm (H) x 24 cm (W) x 11 cm (D) will not be permitted into the stadium, including suitcases. These dimensions are slightly larger than the height and width of an A4 sheet of paper.

Please note that bags cannot be folded to meet the size limit. Stewards will have apparatus to measure bag sizes. Exemptions to the bag policy are available to fans with medical and accessibility requirements. We can also allow exemptions for parents of small children who need provisions such as nappies and bottles with them inside the stadium. If you need an exemption, you should request one as soon as possible by contacting accessibility@brentfordfc.com and providing evidence and information as to why you need a larger bag

Fans with oversized bags that are not permitted into the stadium will be directed to the bag storage facility at the Bees Superstore, located next to the A4/M4.

Prams and buggies can also be stored here.

Bag storage will cost £5 per item for most bags and £10 per item for the largest bags and suitcases. Any profits from the bag storage will be donated to Brentford FC Community Sports Trust

A comprehensive Access Guide is available HERE.

All queries should be directed to Disability Access Officer, Connor Bagenal via the dedicated mailbox at accessibility@brentfordfc.com.

Wheelchair viewing: There are 14 wheelchair spaces available for visiting supporters.

On arrival, you will find a passenger lift that provides access from Thomas Layton Way down to ground level, where the turnstiles are located. Turnstile G is the designated accessible entrance and on the concourse you will have access to a large passenger lift serving the elevated accessible seating areas

Audio Descriptive commentary: Headsets and transmitters are available where required and should be booked in advance by emailing us at accessibility@brentfordfc.com

Away supporters will be able to collect their booked headset from the away end turnstile once into the ground. Please speak to the stewards, who will have the supporters' name and you will be issued with the headset. Please return the headset to a steward when exiting the stadium.

Accessible toilets: There are plenty of high-quality toilet facilities located throughout the stadium, including an ambulant accessible toilet with additional space in each toilet block, as well as separate accessible toilets, all of which are clearly signposted. Within the away end, there are also three accessible toilets available, with one located on the lower concourse and two on the upper concourse. Each accessible toilet is clearly signposted and fitted with a RADAR lock. Supervising stewards carry RADAR keys in case a supporter with access requirements does not have their own.

Assistance Animals: Brentford welcome assistance dogs at the stadium. Please inform them in advance at accessiblity@brentfordfc.com

Smoking, or the use of e-cigarettes is not permitted anywhere across the stadium site.

Everton has a zero-tolerance approach to discriminatory behaviour or language at matches and while travelling to and from fixtures.

The Club’s All Together Now campaign promotes equality, diversity and a football family for everyone.

If you witness or experience any behaviour in the stadium which you believe  falls below the standard of behaviour that you would expect, we encourage you to report it as soon as possible. Please report what you see or experience to any matchday steward, or on WhatsApp* text +442038330327 with details of the incident and our Operations team will be notified. Alternatively, you can email report@brentfordfc.com at any time

Everton supporters can also report discrimination confidentially at: reportit@evertonfc.com

Please consider fellow Evertonians, particularly on concourses.

Behaviour such as throwing beer may result in ejection. More serious incidents may result in arrest and stadium bans.

Everton works with the relevant authorities to identify those responsible for unacceptable behaviour. CCTV can be used as evidence after an incident, even where an individual was not detained on matchday.

Everton does not condone pyrotechnics under any circumstances.

Possession or use may result in Club sanctions, arrest, criminal conviction and a football banning order.

Entering the playing surface without permission is a criminal offence.

Those responsible risk Club sanctions, football bans and criminal consequences which can affect employment, education and international travel.

Please enjoy your matchday and stay safe.

Thank you for your continued support and for helping protect Everton Football Club’s reputation while making the matchday experience enjoyable for everyone.
